title: Short Stuff: Pies
summary: Short Stuff episode on pies. Josh and Chuck trace pie history from ancient Egypt (about 8,000 years ago, gallets made with honey over hot coals) through Greece, Rome, and medieval Europe, where meat pies, pie coffins, and tarts developed and royal pies with live birds were served. They discuss international savory pies (sambusa, pastel-style impignata/pignata, Zwiebelkuchen, tourtière, pork pies). They then cover pumpkin pie (taken to France in 1651 before appearing in America, and in Amelia Simmons' 1796 American Cookery), apple pie (Dutch apple pie predating American apple pie, the "as American as apple pie" phrase, and the WWII "mom and apple pie" saying), cherry pie, Boston cream pie (a cake named for Washington Pie, invented for the 1856 Parker House Hotel opening), Parker House rolls, and key lime pie (Aunt Sally legend in Key West and the condensed milk origin story), ending with lemon icebox pie and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the pie episode and Chuck jokes about pie, mentioning the earlier cake episode and a Paula Tompkins bit on cake versus pie.

segments.title: Ancient and global pie origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe pie origins in Egypt about 8,000 years ago with honey-sweetened gallets cooked over coals, the Greeks replacing sweets with meats and developing pastry dough, and the Romans spreading pie to Europe. They list savory pies from around the world, including sambusa, impignata, Zwiebelkuchen, and tourtière.

segments.title: English pork pies and pie crusts
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss English pork pies, with bones and game bird legs used as handles, and the term coffins for pie crusts.

segments.title: Medieval pie crusts, tarts, and live-bird pies
segments.summary: The hosts explain that medieval pie crusts were often not eaten by the rich, that tarts had no tops, and that early recipes made empty pies. They describe royal pies filled with live birds or musicians, linked to the rhyme Sing a Song of Sixpence, and joke about how the birds got in.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Chuck announces a break before the discussion of specific pies.

segments.title: Pumpkin pie history
segments.summary: Pumpkin pie was brought to the New World, and early versions used pumpkin as the crust. The first recipe for a pumpkin pie appeared in a French cookbook in 1651, and an American recipe appeared in Amelia Simmons' 1796 American Cookery.

segments.title: Apple pie and American identity
segments.summary: The hosts note that apples are native to Asia and Dutch apple pie came centuries earlier. They discuss the phrase 'as American as apple pie,' first used in print in 1928 about Lou Hoover, and the WWII 'mom and apple pie' saying.

segments.title: Cherry pie
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss their preferences for cherry pie served warm and not sour, and note that a cherry pie is said to be among the oldest pies still around, possibly created for Queen Elizabeth I.

segments.title: Boston cream pie and Parker House rolls
segments.summary: Boston cream pie is a cake named for Washington Pie, a cake baked in a pie crust, and was invented for the 1856 opening of the Parker House Hotel. The hosts also discuss Parker House rolls.

segments.title: Key lime pie origins
segments.summary: Key lime pie is described as Florida's pride. One legend credits a woman called Aunt Sally at the Curry House in Key West in the late nineteenth century, adapting a local fishermen's recipe. Another story links it to a 1930s magic lemon cream pie recipe from the Borden Condensed Milk Company.

segments.title: Favorite pies and lemon icebox pie
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh name their favorite pies, including pecan, Dutch apple, and key lime. Chuck describes his grandmother's lemon icebox pie, which has no meringue.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh encourages listeners to go eat pie, and Chuck gives the iHeartRadio production credit and sign-off.
